blocks.body:
How many different necklaces can be made from six beads, each black or white, if two necklaces that differ by a rotation count as the same? There are $2^6 = 64$ colourings, but they do not fall into classes of six: the all-black necklace looks the same after every rotation, while most colourings change under each rotation. The clean way to count is to let the rotation group act on the colourings and count orbits.

Turned inward, with a group acting on itself or on its own subsets, the same counting yields structure theorems, ending with the Sylow theorems, which guarantee subgroups of prime-power order and restrict how many there can be. We use cosets, normal subgroups and centres from [[group-homomorphisms]].

blocks.title: Group action
blocks.body:
An action of a group $G$ on a set $X$ assigns to each $g \in G$ and $x \in X$ an element $g \cdot x \in X$, such that
$$e \cdot x = x \quad \text{and} \quad g \cdot (h \cdot x) = (gh) \cdot x \qquad \text{for all } g, h \in G,\ x \in X.$$
The orbit of $x$ is $G \cdot x = \{g \cdot x : g \in G\}$, and its stabiliser is $G_x = \{g \in G : g \cdot x = x\}$.

Equivalently, an action is a homomorphism from $G$ to the group $\operatorname{Sym}(X)$ of all bijections of $X$: each $g$ becomes the permutation $x \mapsto g \cdot x$, whose inverse is given by $g^{-1}$.

blocks.title: Examples, orbits and stabilisers
blocks.body:
- The rotation group $C_6 = \{r^0, r^1, \dots, r^5\}$ of a hexagon acts on the $64$ black-and-white colourings of its vertices.
- The rotation group of a cube acts on its $6$ faces, on its $8$ vertices and on its $12$ edges.
- Any group acts on itself by left multiplication, $g \cdot x = gx$. Only $e$ acts as the identity permutation, so the homomorphism $G \to \operatorname{Sym}(G)$ is injective: every group of order $n$ is isomorphic to a group of permutations of $n$ objects (Cayley's theorem).
- $G$ acts on itself by conjugation, $g \cdot x = gxg^{-1}$; check that $g \cdot (h \cdot x) = ghxh^{-1}g^{-1} = (gh) \cdot x$. The orbits are the conjugacy classes, and the stabiliser of $x$ is its centraliser $C(x) = \{g : gx = xg\}$.
- If $H \le G$, then $G$ acts on the set of left cosets of $H$ by $g \cdot aH = gaH$.

Two facts are immediate. The stabiliser $G_x$ is a subgroup of $G$. And the orbits partition $X$: the relation "$y = g \cdot x$ for some $g$" is reflexive (take $e$), symmetric (take $g^{-1}$) and transitive (take products).

blocks.title: Orbit–stabiliser theorem
blocks.body:
Let $G$ act on $X$ and let $x \in X$. The map $gG_x \mapsto g \cdot x$ is a well-defined bijection from the set of left cosets of $G_x$ onto the orbit $G \cdot x$. Hence, if $G$ is finite,
$$|G \cdot x| = [G : G_x] = \frac{|G|}{|G_x|}.$$

For $g, h \in G$,
$$g \cdot x = h \cdot x \iff (h^{-1}g) \cdot x = x \iff h^{-1}g \in G_x \iff gG_x = hG_x.$$
Read from right to left, this says the map is well defined; read from left to right, it says the map is injective. Every point $g \cdot x$ of the orbit is the image of $gG_x$, so the map is onto. By Lagrange's theorem the number of left cosets of $G_x$ is $|G|/|G_x|$.

blocks.title: Rotations of a cube
blocks.body: How many rotations does a cube have? Check the answer by counting in two more ways.
blocks.solution:
Let the rotation group $G$ act on the $6$ faces. Any face can be turned to any other, so the orbit of the top face has $6$ elements. A rotation that keeps the top face in place is a rotation about the vertical axis through the centres of the top and bottom faces, by $0^\circ$, $90^\circ$, $180^\circ$ or $270^\circ$, so the stabiliser has $4$ elements. Hence $|G| = 6 \cdot 4 = 24$.

With vertices: all $8$ vertices form one orbit, and the stabiliser of a vertex consists of the $3$ rotations about the long diagonal through it (by $0^\circ$, $120^\circ$, $240^\circ$); $8 \cdot 3 = 24$. With edges: all $12$ edges form one orbit, and an edge is mapped to itself by $2$ rotations, the identity and the half turn about the axis through its midpoint and the midpoint of the opposite edge; $12 \cdot 2 = 24$.

blocks.title: Burnside's lemma
blocks.body:
Let a finite group $G$ act on a finite set $X$, and for $g \in G$ let $\operatorname{Fix}(g) = \{x \in X : g \cdot x = x\}$. Then the number of orbits is
$$\frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{g \in G} |\operatorname{Fix}(g)|.$$

Count the pairs $(g, x)$ with $g \cdot x = x$ in two ways. Grouping by $g$ gives $\sum_g |\operatorname{Fix}(g)|$. Grouping by $x$ gives $\sum_x |G_x| = \sum_x |G|/|G \cdot x|$, by orbit–stabiliser. Split this last sum by orbits: an orbit $O$ contributes $|O|$ terms, each equal to $|G|/|O|$, for a total of $|G|$. So the sum equals $|G|$ times the number of orbits.

(The lemma is older than Burnside and is also called the Cauchy–Frobenius lemma.)

blocks.title: Necklaces
blocks.body: Count the necklaces of six beads, each black or white, up to rotation.
blocks.solution:
The rotation $r^k$, for $k = 0, 1, \dots, 5$, moves bead $i$ to bead $i + k \pmod 6$. Its cycles on the beads all have length $6/\gcd(k, 6)$, so there are $\gcd(k, 6)$ cycles, and a colouring is fixed by $r^k$ exactly when it is constant on each cycle. So $|\operatorname{Fix}(r^k)| = 2^{\gcd(k, 6)}$, which for $k = 0, 1, \dots, 5$ gives
$$64,\ 2,\ 4,\ 8,\ 4,\ 2, \qquad \text{with sum } 84.$$
By Burnside's lemma there are $84/6 = 14$ necklaces.

With a prime number $p$ of beads and $a$ colours, every rotation other than the identity has a single cycle and fixes only the $a$ constant colourings, so there are $\frac{1}{p}\big(a^p + (p - 1)a\big)$ necklaces. That this is an integer means $p \mid a^p - a$: Fermat's little theorem ([[fermat-euler]]), proved by counting.

blocks.title: Conjugation and the class equation
blocks.body:
Now let $G$ act on itself by conjugation. The conjugacy class of $x$ has size $[G : C(x)]$ by orbit–stabiliser; in particular it divides $|G|$. The class of $x$ is just $\{x\}$ exactly when $x$ commutes with everything, that is $x \in Z(G)$. Since the classes partition $G$,
$$|G| = |Z(G)| + \sum_i [G : C(x_i)],$$
where $x_i$ runs over one representative of each class with more than one element. This is the class equation. In the symmetry group $D_4$ of a square (quarter turn $r$, reflection $s$), the classes are $\{e\}, \{r^2\}, \{r, r^3\}, \{s, r^2 s\}, \{rs, r^3 s\}$, and $8 = 2 + (2 + 2 + 2)$.

A $p$-group is a group of order $p^k$ with $p$ prime and $k \ge 1$. Every $p$-group has a nontrivial centre: each index $[G : C(x_i)]$ divides $p^k$ and exceeds $1$, so it is divisible by $p$; so is $|G|$; therefore $p$ divides $|Z(G)|$, and $|Z(G)| \ge p$.

Consequently every group of order $p^2$ is abelian. Its centre has order $p$ or $p^2$. If it had order $p$, then $G/Z(G)$ would have order $p$ and so be cyclic, which by [[group-homomorphisms]] forces $G$ to be abelian, and then $Z(G) = G$, a contradiction. So $Z(G) = G$.

blocks.title: The Sylow theorems
blocks.body:
Let $G$ be a finite group of order $p^a m$, where $p$ is prime, $a \ge 1$ and $p \nmid m$. A subgroup of order $p^a$ is called a Sylow $p$-subgroup.

1. (Existence) $G$ has a Sylow $p$-subgroup.
2. (Conjugacy) Any two Sylow $p$-subgroups $P$ and $Q$ are conjugate: $Q = gPg^{-1}$ for some $g \in G$. Moreover every subgroup of $G$ whose order is a power of $p$ lies inside some Sylow $p$-subgroup.
3. (Counting) The number $n_p$ of Sylow $p$-subgroups satisfies
$$n_p \equiv 1 \pmod p \quad \text{and} \quad n_p \mid m.$$

In particular, by part 2, $n_p = 1$ if and only if the Sylow $p$-subgroup is normal.

We prove part 1, following Wielandt. Let $\Omega$ be the set of all subsets of $G$ with exactly $p^a$ elements, so $|\Omega| = \binom{p^a m}{p^a}$.

First, $p$ does not divide this binomial coefficient. Work with polynomials whose coefficients are taken modulo $p$. Since $p \mid \binom pk$ for $0 < k < p$, we have $(1 + x)^p \equiv 1 + x^p$; applying this $a$ times gives $(1 + x)^{p^a} \equiv 1 + x^{p^a}$, and therefore
$$(1 + x)^{p^a m} \equiv \big(1 + x^{p^a}\big)^m \pmod p.$$
The coefficient of $x^{p^a}$ is $\binom{p^a m}{p^a}$ on the left and $m$ on the right. So $\binom{p^a m}{p^a} \equiv m \not\equiv 0 \pmod p$.

Now let $G$ act on $\Omega$ by left multiplication, $g \cdot S = gS = \{gs : s \in S\}$, which is again a subset with $p^a$ elements. The orbits partition $\Omega$ and $p \nmid |\Omega|$, so some orbit has size not divisible by $p$. Choose $S$ in such an orbit and let $H = G_S = \{g \in G : gS = S\}$.

By orbit–stabiliser, the orbit size $p^a m/|H|$ is not divisible by $p$, so $p^a$ divides $|H|$, and $|H| \ge p^a$. On the other hand, fix some $s \in S$. For $h \in H$ we have $hs \in hS = S$, and $h \mapsto hs$ is injective, so $|H| \le |S| = p^a$. Hence $|H| = p^a$, and $H$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup.

Parts 2 and 3 are standard and we state them without proof; see the references. Both come from conjugation acting on the set of all Sylow $p$-subgroups: letting one Sylow subgroup act gives conjugacy and $n_p \equiv 1 \pmod p$, and then letting all of $G$ act, orbit–stabiliser shows that $n_p$ divides $[G : P] = m$, because the stabiliser of a Sylow subgroup $P$ contains $P$.

blocks.title: Using the Sylow theorems
blocks.body:
Cauchy's theorem follows at once: if a prime $p$ divides $|G|$, then $G$ has an element of order $p$. Take $g \ne e$ in a Sylow $p$-subgroup; its order is $p^j$ with $j \ge 1$, and $g^{p^{j-1}}$ has order $p$.

The counting rules are a recipe for finding normal subgroups: list the divisors $d$ of $m$ with $d \equiv 1 \pmod p$, and if $1$ is the only one, the Sylow $p$-subgroup is normal. They do not always pin $n_p$ down. For $S_4$, of order $24 = 2^3 \cdot 3$, the rules allow $n_2 \in \{1, 3\}$ and $n_3 \in \{1, 4\}$; in fact $n_2 = 3$ (three dihedral subgroups of order $8$) and $n_3 = 4$ (one subgroup generated by a $3$-cycle for each point the $3$-cycle fixes).

blocks.title: Groups of order 15
blocks.body: Show that every group of order $15$ is cyclic.
blocks.solution:
Here $15 = 3 \cdot 5$. The number $n_3$ divides $5$ and is $\equiv 1 \pmod 3$, so $n_3 = 1$; the number $n_5$ divides $3$ and is $\equiv 1 \pmod 5$, so $n_5 = 1$. So there are unique subgroups $P$ of order $3$ and $Q$ of order $5$, both normal, and both cyclic since their orders are prime: $P = \langle x \rangle$, $Q = \langle y \rangle$.

$P \cap Q$ is a subgroup of both, so its order divides $3$ and $5$, and $P \cap Q = \{e\}$. Let $c = xyx^{-1}y^{-1}$. Grouped as $(xyx^{-1})y^{-1}$, it lies in $Q$ because $Q$ is normal; grouped as $x(yx^{-1}y^{-1})$, it lies in $P$ because $P$ is normal. So $c = e$, that is $xy = yx$.

Then $(xy)^k = x^k y^k$, which equals $e$ only if $x^k = y^{-k} \in P \cap Q$, that is $x^k = y^k = e$, which requires $3 \mid k$ and $5 \mid k$. So $xy$ has order $15$, and $G = \langle xy \rangle$ is cyclic.

blocks.title: No simple group of order 30
blocks.body: A group is simple if its only normal subgroups are $\{e\}$ and the group itself. Show that no group of order $30$ is simple.
blocks.solution:
We have $30 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$. The divisors of $10$ that are $\equiv 1 \pmod 3$ are $1$ and $10$, so $n_3 \in \{1, 10\}$; the divisors of $6$ that are $\equiv 1 \pmod 5$ are $1$ and $6$, so $n_5 \in \{1, 6\}$. If $n_3 = 1$ or $n_5 = 1$, that Sylow subgroup is normal, of order $3$ or $5$, and $G$ is not simple.

Suppose instead $n_3 = 10$ and $n_5 = 6$. Two distinct subgroups of order $3$ intersect in a subgroup of order dividing $3$ that is not the whole of either, so they share only $e$. Each contains $2$ elements of order $3$, and every element of order $3$ lies in exactly one of them (the one it generates), so $G$ has $10 \cdot 2 = 20$ elements of order $3$. In the same way the six subgroups of order $5$ give $6 \cdot 4 = 24$ elements of order $5$. That makes $44 > 30$ elements, which is absurd. So $G$ has a normal subgroup of order $3$ or $5$.

blocks.body:
- The converse of Lagrange's theorem is false: $A_4$ has order $12$ but no subgroup of order $6$. Sylow's theorem guarantees subgroups of prime-power order only.
- Burnside's lemma averages numbers of fixed points; it does not say the orbits have equal size. Dividing $64$ by $6$ in the necklace problem is meaningless.
- Right multiplication, $g \cdot x = xg$, is not a left action unless $G$ is abelian: it gives $g \cdot (h \cdot x) = xhg$ instead of $xgh$. Use $g \cdot x = xg^{-1}$.
- In the counting rule, $n_p$ divides $m$, the part of $|G|$ prime to $p$; using only $n_p \mid |G|$ throws information away.
- Element counting as in the order-$30$ example needs subgroups of prime order. Distinct Sylow subgroups of order $p^2$ or more can share nonidentity elements.

Burnside's lemma, refined to record how many beads of each colour are used, becomes Pólya enumeration, a standard tool of [[counting]] that packages answers as [[generating-functions]]. Groups acting on the roots of a polynomial are the subject of [[galois]] theory, where Cauchy's theorem is used to find elements of prescribed order in a Galois group. The congruence $\binom{p^a m}{p^a} \equiv m \pmod p$ in Wielandt's proof is a special case of [[lucas]]. In geometry, symmetry groups of figures act on their points ([[geo-transformations]]), and orbit–stabiliser computes their orders as it did for the cube.

1. In how many ways can the faces of a cube be coloured with $3$ colours, up to rotation? (Sort the $24$ rotations by type first.)
2. Let $G$ be a group of order $p^k$ acting on a finite set $X$, and let $X^G$ be the set of points fixed by every element of $G$. Show that $|X| \equiv |X^G| \pmod p$.
3. Show that every group of order $35$ is cyclic.
4. Show that a group of order $56$ has a normal Sylow $2$-subgroup or a normal Sylow $7$-subgroup.

sources.ref: Rotman, An Introduction to the Theory of Groups
